title: IgA Nephropathy
subject: Pathology
summary: IgA nephropathy is a primary glomerulonephritis with mesangial IgA deposits, often presenting with episodic hematuria after respiratory infections. It progresses slowly, with proteinuria and hypertension as key prognostic markers.

sections.p: IgA nephropathy is the most common primary glomerulonephritis worldwide. It is diagnosed by kidney biopsy showing mesangial IgA and C3 deposition on immunofluorescence, with no systemic disease.

sections.p: The exact trigger is unknown, but infections, especially upper respiratory tract infections, are the most common precipitating events. Tropical infections and endemic diseases can also contribute.
b: Upper respiratory tract infection (viral or bacterial)

t.b: Elevated galactose‑deficient IgA1 is characteristic but not routinely measured

sections.p: Patients usually have painless gross or microscopic hematuria that peaks 1–2 weeks after a respiratory infection. Proteinuria and hypertension develop later.

t.b: Hypertension indicates worsening renal involvement

sections.p: In low‑resource settings, focus on urine microscopy, basic biochemistry, and renal ultrasound. Advanced tests are optional.

sections.p: Treat underlying infection, control blood pressure, and reduce proteinuria. ACE inhibitors or ARBs are first line; steroids are reserved for rapidly progressive disease.

faq.q: Can IgA nephropathy resolve on its own?
faq.a: In many cases, hematuria resolves after the inciting infection, but proteinuria and kidney function decline may persist.
Yes, familial clustering suggests a genetic predisposition, but specific genes are not routinely tested.

faq.q: What is the role of diet?
faq.a: Low sodium and protein restriction may help reduce proteinuria and hypertension.

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with painless hematuria 10 days after a sore throat – what is the most likely diagnosis? — IgA nephropathy; key points: episodic hematuria post‑respiratory infection, normal complement, mesangial IgA on biopsy.
Which investigation is most useful when a renal biopsy is unavailable? — Urine microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs; key points: confirms glomerular source.
A patient with IgA nephropathy develops proteinuria >3.5 g/day – what is the first drug to start? — ACE inhibitor or ARB; key points: reduces proteinuria, slows progression.
Why are steroids reserved for only some IgA nephropathy patients? — They are used in rapidly progressive forms with crescents; risk of infection and side effects.
What lab value would differentiate post‑streptococcal GN from IgA nephropathy? — Low serum C3; key points: complement low in post‑streptococcal, normal in IgA.

In a low‑resource setting, how would you monitor disease progression? — Serial serum creatinine, eGFR, and urine protein/creatinine ratio every 3–6 months; key points: track kidney function and proteinuria.
